name: Adobe’s media cache
answer: Yes. The media cache is audio and video that Premiere, After Effects and Media Encoder processed so previews play smoothly, and Adobe says deleted cache files are recreated automatically when your media needs them.
comes_back: Yes, for any project you open again. Cache made for footage you’ve since deleted never comes back, which is why clearing it pays.

name: After Effects’ disk cache
answer: Yes. The disk cache is frames After Effects already rendered, kept so previews don’t render them again.
comes_back: Yes. The disk cache is on by default and fills again as you preview.

name: Android emulators (AVDs)
answer: Yes, the ones you don’t use, from Android Studio’s Device Manager.
comes_back: Only as a new, empty device you create again. Its apps, sign-ins and snapshots don’t come back.

name: The Android SDK
answer: No, not all of it while you build Android apps: Android Studio, Gradle and the emulator all run from it.
comes_back: Only by downloading it again. Delete the whole SDK and Android Studio can’t build or run apps until you reinstall it.

name: App data (Application Support)
answer: No, not as a whole.
comes_back: Only as an empty folder. An app creates a fresh one the next time it runs, but the old contents are gone.

name: macOS downloads (AssetsV2)
answer: No. AssetsV2 is where macOS keeps parts it downloads after it’s installed: Apple Intelligence and Siri models, voices, dictionaries, fonts, security data and software updates on their way in.
comes_back: Yes. macOS manages what’s in it, adding and replacing assets as features and updates need them.

name: Bun’s cache (~/.bun)
answer: Yes, the cache part.
comes_back: Yes, with every bun install.

name: Cargo’s registry and git cache
answer: Yes, those two. They’re Cargo’s cache of crates and git dependencies, which Cargo extracts or downloads again.
comes_back: Yes. Since Rust 1.88, Cargo also trims old cache files by itself.

name: Google Chrome’s cache
answer: Yes. Chrome’s cache is parts of pages it saved so sites open faster.
comes_back: Yes, as you browse. Chrome refills it by itself, so clearing it fixes problems more than it frees space for good.

name: Chrome’s on-device AI model
answer: Not by hand. The folder holds Gemini Nano, the AI model Chrome keeps on your Mac for features like help with writing and scam warnings.
comes_back: After a manual delete it can, while On-device AI is on. Turn that off in Chrome’s Settings › AI Innovations and Chrome deletes the model and stops downloading it.

name: Claude Code’s ~/.claude folder
answer: No, not all of it.
comes_back: New data is written as you use Claude Code; deleted transcripts and settings aren’t. Claude Code already deletes transcripts older than 30 days on its own.

name: CocoaPods’ cache and Pods
answer: Yes, all three come back with pod install.
comes_back: Yes, at the versions recorded in Podfile.lock.

name: Codex’s ~/.codex folder
answer: Partly. ~/.codex is the Codex CLI’s home: your config.toml, possibly your login, and every session it has saved.
comes_back: New sessions are written as you work. Deleted ones don’t come back, and Codex keeps every session until you archive or delete it.

name: conda’s pkgs and environments
answer: Yes, through conda. conda clean --all removes cached packages no environment uses, along with tarballs, index caches and logs.
comes_back: The cache refills as you install. Environments are different: one you remove is gone unless you exported it first.

name: Sandboxed apps’ data (Containers)
answer: No, not the folder, and not the container of an app you use.
comes_back: As a fresh, empty container the next time the app opens; the old contents don’t.

name: Cursor’s extensions (~/.cursor)
answer: No, not by hand.
comes_back: Extensions come back only when you install them again, and a deleted mcp.json doesn’t come back at all.

name: Cursor’s update cache (ShipIt)
answer: Yes, with Cursor quit.
comes_back: Yes, the next time Cursor updates itself.

name: DaVinci Resolve’s render cache
answer: Yes. CacheClip holds render cache: clips, effects and grades Resolve already rendered so playback stays smooth.
comes_back: Yes, as you work with render caching on. Optimized and proxy media, kept nearby, come back only when you generate them again.

name: Removed accounts (Deleted Users)
answer: Yes, once you’ve checked it.
comes_back: No. Once the image is deleted and the Trash emptied, the account can’t be restored from it.

name: Crash reports (DiagnosticReports)
answer: Yes. Every file in it is a report macOS wrote after something crashed, hung or ran into trouble.
comes_back: Only when something fails again. A folder that refills quickly is a symptom worth fixing, not just clearing.

name: Discord’s cache
answer: Yes, with Discord fully quit.
comes_back: Yes, as you use Discord. Clearing only the three cache folders leaves the rest of Discord’s local data alone; Discord’s own reinstall steps remove the whole folder.

name: Docker Desktop’s Docker.raw
answer: No, not as a way to free space.
comes_back: Docker Desktop starts again with an empty disk. What was in it doesn’t come back.

name: Document versions (.DocumentRevisions-V100)
answer: Leave the folder itself.
comes_back: Yes: macOS keeps saving versions as you work, every hour and whenever you save, rename or duplicate a document.

name: ._ files (AppleDouble) and dot_clean
answer: Yes, on a drive that goes into a TV, car stereo, camera or Windows PC.
comes_back: Yes, whenever a Mac copies or changes files on that drive again. dot_clean, built into macOS, clears them.

name: The Downloads folder
answer: Yes, whatever you no longer need.
comes_back: Not by itself. A deleted download returns only if you download it again, and not every link works twice.

name: Dropbox’s cache folder
answer: Yes, with Dropbox quit.
comes_back: Yes, as Dropbox syncs. Dropbox suggests clearing it by hand only to remove sensitive files at once or to free space now.

name: .DS_Store files
answer: Yes. A .DS_Store file only remembers how Finder shows its folder: the view, where icons sit and similar settings.
comes_back: Yes. Finder writes a new one when it opens the folder again, so clearing them is mainly for folders you share.

name: The dyld shared cache
answer: No. The dyld shared cache is where macOS keeps all of its system libraries, the code every app on your Mac runs on.
comes_back: It’s replaced with each macOS update and never needs cleaning by hand. There’s nothing to win here.

name: Final Cut Pro’s render files
answer: Yes, from inside Final Cut Pro.
comes_back: Yes. Final Cut renders in the background by default, and Modify › Render All renders on demand.

name: Firefox’s cache
answer: Yes. Mozilla’s own documentation says this folder is for caches that can safely be deleted.
comes_back: Yes. Firefox fills it again as you browse, and it can empty it each time it closes if you ask it to.

name: Dart and Flutter’s pub cache
answer: Yes. It’s pub’s system cache of packages downloaded for your Dart and Flutter projects.
comes_back: Yes, package by package, as projects fetch them.

name: Font caches
answer: Yes, with Apple’s tools.
comes_back: Yes. macOS builds new databases from the fonts in the standard font folders after you log out or restart.

name: File change logs (.fseventsd)
answer: No, leave it. .fseventsd is macOS’s running record of which folders changed on a disk.
comes_back: At once: macOS’s fseventsd service keeps writing it as files change.

name: GarageBand and Logic sound library
answer: Yes, if you don’t make music on this Mac.
comes_back: Only if you download it again, from GarageBand › Sound Library or Logic Pro › Sound Library.

name: A project’s .git folder
answer: Usually not. .git is the repository itself: every commit, branch, tag and stash of the project.
comes_back: Only by cloning from a remote, and only what you pushed. To get space back, make the repository smaller with Git’s own tools instead.

name: Go’s module and build caches
answer: Yes, with Go’s own commands.
comes_back: Yes. The build cache trims itself; the module cache only grows until you clean it.

name: Google Drive’s cache (DriveFS)
answer: Leave it. DriveFS is Google Drive for desktop’s cache, and Google’s admin documentation says files are moved there before they’re uploaded.
comes_back: Yes, Drive rebuilds it. To use less space, stream files instead of mirroring them, and keep fewer files available offline.

name: Gradle’s caches (~/.gradle)
answer: Yes, with Gradle stopped.
comes_back: Yes. Gradle also prunes these folders itself, so clearing by hand is mainly for getting space back now.

name: Shared app data (Group Containers)
answer: No. Each folder here holds data that several apps from one developer share, or that an app shares with its widgets and extensions.
comes_back: As an empty folder if any app in the group runs again; what was in it doesn’t.

name: Homebrew’s cache and old versions
answer: Yes. It holds bottles and installers Homebrew already downloaded; what you’ve installed runs from elsewhere.
comes_back: Yes. Every install and upgrade adds downloads, and Homebrew trims them on its own schedule.

name: The Hugging Face cache
answer: Yes, but pick what goes.
comes_back: Yes: when code asks for a model or dataset that isn’t cached, it downloads it again.

name: iCloud Drive’s local copies
answer: Only with Remove Download.
comes_back: A removed download comes back when you open the file. A deleted file comes back only from Recently Deleted on iCloud.com, for 30 days.

name: iMovie render files
answer: Yes, with iMovie’s own Delete button.
comes_back: Yes. iMovie makes new render files as you edit, so they build up again with each project.

name: Xcode iOS DeviceSupport
answer: Yes, with Xcode quit, and especially the folders for iOS versions none of your devices run any more.
comes_back: Yes, for each device you plug in again. Folders for iOS versions you no longer use simply don’t come back.

name: iPhone and iPad update files (.ipsw)
paths: ~/Library/iTunes/iPhone Software Updates; ~/Library/iTunes/iPad Software Updates; ~/Library/iTunes/iPod Software Updates
answer: Yes. An .ipsw file is a copy of iOS or iPadOS your Mac downloaded to update or restore a device.
comes_back: Yes, when it’s needed: the Mac downloads the software again for the next update or restore.

name: JetBrains IDE caches
answer: Yes, with the IDE quit.
comes_back: Yes, as soon as you open a project in that IDE again.

name: Keychains folder
answer: No. ~/Library/Keychains holds your login keychain and this Mac’s copy of your iCloud Keychain or Local Items: saved passwords, passkeys, certificates and private keys.
comes_back: Not by itself. Passwords you sync with iCloud Keychain are still in iCloud, but anything kept only on this Mac needs a backup to come back.

name: Your caches folder (~/Library/Caches)
answer: Yes, app by app, with each app quit.
comes_back: Yes. It starts refilling as soon as you use your apps, so clearing it buys space for a while rather than for good.

name: Log files (~/Library/Logs)
answer: Yes, your old ones.
comes_back: New logs appear as apps keep writing; the old ones are gone for good. “All logs” isn’t something you can or need to delete: macOS’s main log is managed by macOS, which trims it itself.

name: Lightroom Classic’s previews
answer: Yes, with Lightroom Classic quit.
comes_back: Yes, folder by folder, as you open them.

name: LM Studio models
answer: Yes, model by model.
comes_back: Only by downloading it again.

name: Old macOS installers
paths: /Applications/Install macOS Tahoe.app; /Applications/Install macOS Sequoia.app; ~/Applications/Install macOS Sonoma.app
answer: Yes, the installers. An app named “Install macOS …” in Applications is a full macOS installer that was downloaded and never removed.
comes_back: Only if you download it again, from Software Update, the App Store or Apple’s download page.

name: Mail’s data folder
answer: No. ~/Library/Mail is Mail’s copy of your email: every mailbox, message and downloaded attachment, including mailboxes kept On My Mac and POP mail that may exist nowhere else.
comes_back: Only what’s still on the servers. To make Mail smaller, work from inside Mail with the steps below.

name: Mail Downloads
answer: Yes, for attachments you only opened.
comes_back: Only for attachments you open again. Mail also clears unedited copies on its own, by default when you delete the email they came from.

name: Maven’s local repository (~/.m2)
answer: Mostly. Nearly everything in it is libraries and plugins Maven downloaded, and those come back on the next build.
comes_back: Yes, as you build.

name: Messages attachments
answer: Yes, if you can live without them, and if you delete them in Messages or Storage settings rather than in the folder.
comes_back: No, unless you saved a copy elsewhere or have a backup. Treat it as gone.

name: Microsoft Teams’ cache
answer: Yes, with Teams quit.
comes_back: Yes, the next time Teams opens.

name: Next.js .next folders
answer: Yes, with the dev server stopped.
comes_back: Yes, on the next next dev or next build.

name: node_modules folders
answer: Yes, in projects you aren’t running right now.
comes_back: Yes, the same tree as before, when you run npm install (or yarn, pnpm install, bun install) against the project’s lockfile.

name: npm’s cache (~/.npm)
answer: Yes. ~/.npm only holds copies of packages npm has already downloaded, plus logs and tools fetched by npx.
comes_back: Yes. npm adds to it with every install and never removes anything on its own.

name: Ollama models
answer: Yes, with ollama rm.
comes_back: Only with ollama pull. Layers another model still uses are already on your Mac and don’t download again.

name: Parallels virtual machines (.pvm)
answer: Yes, if you’re done with everything inside it.
comes_back: No. A new virtual machine means installing its operating system again; only a copy or backup you made brings the old one back.

name: The Photos library
answer: No, not the library itself.
comes_back: Photos you delete in Photos wait 30 days in Recently Deleted. A library deleted in Finder comes back only from a backup; with iCloud Photos, what had finished uploading is still in iCloud.

name: pip’s cache
answer: Yes. It’s pip’s download cache plus wheels it built, kept so the next install is faster.
comes_back: Yes, with each pip install.

name: pnpm’s store
answer: Yes, by pruning it.
comes_back: The store refills with every pnpm install, so prune it now and then.

name: Downloaded podcast episodes
answer: Yes. A downloaded episode is a copy for listening offline.
comes_back: Only if you download it again, or automatic downloads fetch new episodes, which is what fills the space up again.

name: Settings files (.plist in Preferences)
answer: Not all of them.
comes_back: A fresh file with default settings appears as soon as the app runs again; your old choices don’t.

name: __pycache__ folders
answer: Yes. Every file in __pycache__ is compiled from a .py file beside it, and Python compiles it again by itself.
comes_back: Yes, as soon as the code runs again, unless you tell Python not to write these files.

name: Python virtual environments
answer: Yes, if the project lists its packages.
comes_back: Yes, when you recreate it from requirements.txt, pyproject.toml or a lockfile.

name: Quick Look’s thumbnail cache
answer: Yes. It holds the little previews Finder shows instead of plain icons for photos, PDFs, videos and documents.
comes_back: Yes, by itself. Quick Look makes new thumbnails as you browse, so the cache fills up again.

name: Rust target folders
answer: Yes. target is everything Cargo compiled for the project, and none of it is source.
comes_back: Yes, with the next cargo build, cargo test or editor check.

name: Safari’s cache and website data
answer: Yes. The cache is copies of pages, images and scripts Safari saved so sites open faster, and Safari fetches them again as you browse.
comes_back: Yes, the cache refills as you browse. Clear it from Safari’s own settings rather than by deleting folders.

name: Saved windows (Saved Application State)
answer: Yes. It only remembers which windows each app had open, and where, so they reappear when you reopen the app or restart the Mac.
comes_back: Yes. Apps write their saved state again as you use them, unless you turn the feature off.

name: Slack’s cache
answer: Yes. Your messages, files and channels are kept in your Slack workspaces; the Mac app stores copies so it opens quickly.
comes_back: Yes, as soon as Slack runs.

name: The sleep image (sleepimage)
answer: No, leave it. It’s where macOS saves a copy of memory so a sleeping Mac can pick up where it was, even if the battery runs out.
comes_back: Yes, by itself. On a laptop it’s part of normal sleep.

name: Spotify’s cache and downloads
answer: Yes, the cache. It’s parts of songs and podcasts Spotify saved so they play without stalling, and Clear cache in Spotify’s settings removes it safely.
comes_back: The cache does, as you listen. Downloads only come back if you download them again.

name: The Spotlight index (.Spotlight-V100)
answer: Not by hand. .Spotlight-V100 is one disk’s search index, the thing Spotlight, Finder’s search, Mail’s search and many apps look things up in.
comes_back: Yes: Spotlight indexes the disk again, and the index grows back to fit what’s on it.

name: Steam games and the Steam folder
answer: Mostly. A game you bought stays in your Steam library and can be installed again.
comes_back: The game, yes, by installing it again. Saves only if they’re in Steam Cloud or you backed them up.

name: Swap files (swapfile)
answer: No. Swap files hold parts of memory macOS moved to the disk to make room.
comes_back: Whenever memory runs short again. A lot of swap is a sign the Mac needs more memory for what you ask of it, not a cleaning problem.

name: Swift Package Manager caches
answer: Yes. The shared cache in ~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm and each package’s .build folder are fetched or built again.
comes_back: Yes, at the versions pinned in Package.resolved.

name: System-wide caches (/Library/Caches)
answer: No, leave it to macOS.
comes_back: Yes. Whatever is cleared is rebuilt as it’s needed, which is the other reason clearing it rarely pays.

name: Telegram’s media cache
answer: Yes. Telegram stores your chats and media in its cloud, and what’s on your Mac is a cache.
comes_back: Yes. Telegram says media removed from the cache stays in the cloud and downloads again the moment you open it.

name: The Trash
answer: Yes, once you’ve looked through it.
comes_back: No. Only a backup made before can bring an emptied item back. The Trash itself fills up again as you delete things.

name: UTM virtual machines (.utm)
answer: Yes, when you no longer need the guest.
comes_back: No. Export or clone a VM first if you might want it later.

name: uv’s cache (~/.cache/uv)
answer: Yes, with uv’s commands.
comes_back: Yes, as soon as uv installs anything.

name: Temporary files (/private/var/folders)
answer: No, not by hand.
comes_back: All the time: everything that runs uses it, so it’s never empty, and isn’t meant to be.

name: VirtualBox virtual machines
answer: Yes, VM by VM, from VirtualBox.
comes_back: No. Copy or export a VM first if you might need it again.

name: VS Code’s caches and extensions
answer: Yes, the caches, with VS Code quit.
comes_back: Yes. The caches refill as you work, and each extension update adds a new version folder.

name: WhatsApp’s media and data
answer: Be careful. WhatsApp for Mac holds a copy of your recent chats and the photos, videos and files in them.
comes_back: Only what your phone still has. When you link a Mac, your phone sends it your recent history.

name: Xcode Archives
answer: Partly. Archives of builds nobody runs any more can go.
comes_back: No. Archiving the same code again makes a new build with a different build UUID, and a dSYM only works with the binary it was made with.

name: Xcode simulators (CoreSimulator)
answer: Yes, with Xcode’s own tools.
comes_back: A simulator is added again in Xcode in moments, empty. A runtime comes back from Xcode › Settings › Components.

name: Yarn’s cache
answer: Yes, with one exception.
comes_back: Yes, with every install.

name: Zoom recordings and cache
answer: Your call. A computer recording is a video Zoom made on this Mac, and it may be the only copy: Zoom’s help notes it can only be played on the device where it was made.
comes_back: No. Zoom’s cache is a different matter: Zoom’s own help has you move its data folder to the Trash.
